name: Atrial Fibrillation
tagline: Disorganised atrial electrical activity that abolishes effective atrial contraction, producing an irregularly irregular ventricular response and a substantial risk of stroke.
overview: Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained arrhythmia in clinical practice. Coordinated atrial depolarisation is replaced by rapid, chaotic electrical activity, so the atria quiver rather than contract. The atrioventricular node filters this chaotic input, producing an irregularly irregular ventricular response. Two consequences dominate management: loss of the atrial contribution to ventricular filling, which reduces cardiac output particularly when the ventricle is stiff or the rate is fast; and stasis of blood in the fibrillating atrium, especially the left atrial appendage, which predisposes to thrombus formation and cardioembolic stroke. Management rests on three pillars — anticoagulation guided by stroke risk, symptom control by rate or rhythm strategy, and treatment of the underlying substrate and risk factors.

modifiable: Physical inactivity, and also extreme endurance exercise
Heart failure and valvular heart disease
Acute illness, sepsis, surgery and electrolyte disturbance
nonModifiable: Increasing age — the dominant risk factor

pathophysiology.title: Substrate development
pathophysiology.text: Atrial stretch, fibrosis, inflammation and ageing alter atrial structure and electrophysiology. Conduction becomes slow and heterogeneous, and refractory periods shorten and disperse — the substrate on which fibrillation can be sustained.

pathophysiology.title: Triggering ectopy
pathophysiology.text: Rapidly firing foci, most often within the myocardial sleeves of the pulmonary veins, generate premature atrial beats that initiate the arrhythmia. This is the observation that made pulmonary vein isolation possible.

pathophysiology.title: Multiple re-entrant wavelets
pathophysiology.text: Once initiated, multiple simultaneous re-entrant wavelets and rotors propagate through the atria in continually changing directions, producing atrial rates of roughly 300–600 per minute.

pathophysiology.title: Loss of coordinated contraction
pathophysiology.text: Because activation is disorganised, the atria never contract as a unit. The atrial kick is lost, reducing ventricular filling by up to 20–30% — more when the ventricle is non-compliant.

pathophysiology.title: Irregular ventricular response
pathophysiology.text: The AV node conducts some impulses and blocks others through decremental conduction and concealed conduction, producing the irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm. Without treatment the rate is often 100–160 per minute.

pathophysiology.title: Haemodynamic consequences
pathophysiology.text: Loss of atrial kick plus a rapid, irregular rate shortens diastolic filling time and reduces cardiac output. Sustained tachycardia can itself cause a reversible tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy.

pathophysiology.title: Thrombus formation
pathophysiology.text: Stasis in the fibrillating atrium — particularly the trabeculated, narrow-necked left atrial appendage — combines with endothelial dysfunction and a prothrombotic state (Virchow's triad) to promote thrombus, the source of cardioembolic stroke.

pathophysiology.title: Atrial remodelling
pathophysiology.text: Fibrillation itself shortens atrial refractoriness and promotes further fibrosis and dilatation — 'atrial fibrillation begets atrial fibrillation' — so paroxysmal episodes tend to become persistent over time.

anatomyInvolved: Left atrium and its myocardium, the principal site of the arrhythmic substrate
Pulmonary vein sleeves, the dominant source of triggers
Left atrial appendage, the main site of thrombus formation
Atrioventricular node, which determines the ventricular response
Left ventricle, whose filling depends partly on atrial contraction
physiologyChanges: Loss of the atrial contribution to ventricular filling, reducing stroke volume
Shortened and variable diastolic filling time with rapid, irregular ventricular response
Beat-to-beat variation in stroke volume, producing a pulse deficit between apical and radial rates
Elevated left atrial pressure and progressive atrial dilatation
Electrical remodelling with shortened atrial refractory periods
Prothrombotic milieu within the atrium

progression.text: The first documented episode, regardless of duration or symptoms.
Episodes that terminate spontaneously or with intervention within seven days, usually trigger-driven.
Episodes sustained beyond seven days, or requiring cardioversion to terminate. Reflects a more developed substrate.
Continuous atrial fibrillation for a year or more where a rhythm control strategy is still being pursued.
Atrial fibrillation accepted by patient and clinician, with no further attempts at rhythm control. A therapeutic decision rather than a pathological stage.

symptoms: Palpitations, often described as an irregular or racing heartbeat
Fatigue, dizziness and, less commonly, syncope
Entirely asymptomatic in a substantial proportion — the first presentation may be stroke or heart failure
signs: Irregularly irregular pulse — the defining bedside sign
Apical–radial pulse deficit from beats too weak to generate a palpable pulse
Variable intensity of the first heart sound
Absent a waves in the jugular venous pulse
Signs of heart failure, thyrotoxicosis or valve disease as underlying causes

investigations.findings: Absent P waves replaced by a fibrillatory baseline, with an irregularly irregular QRS rhythm. A single documented ECG is sufficient for diagnosis.
Holter monitoring, event recorders, patch monitors or implantable loop recorders to capture paroxysmal episodes and assess rate control.
Left atrial size, ventricular function, and valve disease — particularly rheumatic mitral stenosis, which changes anticoagulation decisions.
The standard for excluding left atrial appendage thrombus before cardioversion or ablation when anticoagulation has not been adequate.
Thyroid function, full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes — both to find causes and to guide anticoagulant dosing.
Validated stroke risk scores guide anticoagulation, and bleeding risk assessment identifies modifiable bleeding factors rather than reasons to withhold therapy.

complications: Ischaemic stroke and systemic thromboembolism
Heart failure, including tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy
Reduced exercise capacity and quality of life
Cognitive decline and vascular dementia
Bleeding as a complication of anticoagulation
Increased all-cause mortality

treatment.principles: Modern management follows a structured approach: assess and treat stroke risk with anticoagulation, control symptoms with a rate or rhythm strategy, and address the substrate through comorbidity and risk factor management. Aspirin is not an adequate substitute for anticoagulation for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation. This is an educational summary; management must follow current guidelines and individual assessment.

groups.name: Stroke prevention
groups.detail: Oral anticoagulation based on validated stroke risk assessment; direct oral anticoagulants are preferred over vitamin K antagonists for most patients, with warfarin retained for mechanical valves and moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis.

groups.name: Rate control
groups.detail: Beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers or digoxin to control the ventricular response.

groups.name: Rhythm control — pharmacological
groups.detail: Antiarrhythmic drugs selected according to the presence and type of structural heart disease.

groups.name: Cardioversion
groups.detail: Electrical or pharmacological restoration of sinus rhythm, with attention to anticoagulation timing and thrombus exclusion.

groups.name: Catheter ablation
groups.detail: Pulmonary vein isolation, increasingly offered early in symptomatic patients and of particular benefit in atrial fibrillation with heart failure.

groups.name: Left atrial appendage occlusion
groups.detail: Considered for patients with a genuine long-term contraindication to anticoagulation.

groups.name: Risk factor management
groups.detail: Weight reduction, treatment of sleep apnoea, blood pressure control, alcohol reduction and exercise — all shown to reduce arrhythmia burden.

keyTakeaways: The commonest sustained arrhythmia; incidence rises steeply with age.
ECG diagnosis: absent P waves with an irregularly irregular ventricular response.
Most triggers arise from pulmonary vein myocardial sleeves — the rationale for pulmonary vein isolation.
Loss of the atrial kick can reduce cardiac output by 20–30%, and matters most when the ventricle is stiff.
The left atrial appendage is the dominant source of thrombus and of cardioembolic stroke.
Anticoagulation decisions rest on stroke risk, not on the pattern or symptoms of the arrhythmia.
Atrial fibrillation begets atrial fibrillation — remodelling makes episodes progressively more sustained.

name: Supraventricular Tachycardia
tagline: Regular, rapid tachycardias arising above the ventricles — most commonly re-entrant circuits involving the AV node or an accessory pathway.
overview: Supraventricular tachycardia describes regular tachycardias whose maintenance depends on tissue at or above the level of the bundle of His. The two commonest forms are atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia, which uses dual pathways within and adjacent to the AV node, and atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia, which uses an accessory pathway connecting atrium and ventricle — the mechanism underlying Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome. Atrial tachycardia and atrial flutter are also supraventricular. Most SVT is not life-threatening, but it can be highly symptomatic, and pre-excited atrial fibrillation in Wolff–Parkinson–White is genuinely dangerous.

pathophysiology.title: Dual pathway physiology
pathophysiology.text: In AVNRT, the AV node region has a fast pathway with a long refractory period and a slow pathway with a short refractory period.

pathophysiology.title: Initiation by a premature beat
pathophysiology.text: A premature atrial beat arrives when the fast pathway is still refractory, so it conducts down the slow pathway alone.

pathophysiology.title: Re-entry established
pathophysiology.text: By the time the impulse reaches the distal node, the fast pathway has recovered and conducts retrogradely to the atrium, completing a circuit that then perpetuates itself.

pathophysiology.title: Accessory pathway variant
pathophysiology.text: In AVRT, the circuit uses the AV node in one direction and an accessory pathway in the other. Orthodromic conduction gives a narrow QRS; antidromic conduction gives a wide one.

pathophysiology.title: Haemodynamic effect
pathophysiology.text: Rapid rates shorten diastolic filling, reducing stroke volume. Simultaneous atrial and ventricular contraction against closed AV valves produces cannon a waves and the sensation of neck pounding.

pathophysiology.title: Danger in pre-excited AF
pathophysiology.text: If atrial fibrillation occurs in a patient with an accessory pathway that lacks decremental properties, very rapid ventricular rates can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation.

anatomyInvolved: Atrioventricular node and its fast and slow pathway inputs
Accessory atrioventricular connections such as the bundle of Kent
Atrial myocardium in focal atrial tachycardia
Cavotricuspid isthmus in typical atrial flutter
physiologyChanges: Sustained rapid regular rate, typically 150–250 per minute
Shortened diastolic filling time reducing stroke volume
Loss of normal atrioventricular timing
Reduced coronary perfusion time, which may provoke angina
Ventricular pre-excitation with a delta wave in sinus rhythm in Wolff–Parkinson–White

progression.text: Sudden onset and offset episodes, often since adolescence, with long asymptomatic intervals.
Episodes become more frequent or prolonged, affecting daily life and work.
Rarely, incessant tachycardia causes a tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy; pre-excited atrial fibrillation risks sudden death.
Catheter ablation offers high cure rates and is increasingly chosen early rather than after years of drug therapy.

symptoms: Polyuria after termination, from natriuretic peptide release
signs: Regular rapid pulse, typically 150–250 per minute
Cannon a waves in the jugular venous pulse — the frog sign
Usually normal blood pressure, but hypotension if rate is very fast or there is structural disease
Termination with vagal manoeuvres or adenosine

investigations.findings: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia; retrograde P waves may be buried in or distort the QRS (pseudo-R′ in V1, pseudo-S in inferior leads).
May reveal a short PR interval with a delta wave, indicating ventricular pre-excitation.
Captures paroxysmal episodes and documents onset and offset.
Excludes structural heart disease, particularly Ebstein's anomaly, which is associated with accessory pathways.
Defines the mechanism precisely and permits ablation in the same procedure.

complications: Syncope and injury
Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy
Ventricular fibrillation in pre-excited atrial fibrillation
Marked impairment of quality of life
Procedural risk of AV block during ablation near the node

treatment.principles: Acute termination uses vagal manoeuvres and AV nodal blockade; long-term management balances drug therapy against catheter ablation, which is often curative. AV nodal blocking drugs must be avoided in pre-excited atrial fibrillation. Educational summary only.

groups.name: Vagal manoeuvres
groups.detail: Valsalva — particularly the modified Valsalva — and carotid sinus massage in appropriate patients.

groups.name: Adenosine
groups.detail: Transient AV nodal block that terminates node-dependent tachycardias and unmasks atrial arrhythmias.

groups.name: Rate-slowing drugs
groups.detail: Beta-blockers and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers for acute and chronic management of node-dependent SVT.

groups.name: Synchronised cardioversion
groups.detail: For haemodynamic instability, and in pre-excited atrial fibrillation.

groups.name: Catheter ablation
groups.detail: Slow pathway modification for AVNRT and accessory pathway ablation for AVRT, with high success and low complication rates.

keyTakeaways: AVNRT is the commonest regular SVT; AVRT uses an accessory pathway.
Sudden onset and offset with neck pounding is a classic history.
Adenosine both terminates node-dependent SVT and reveals atrial arrhythmias.
Avoid AV nodal blocking drugs in pre-excited atrial fibrillation — they can precipitate ventricular fibrillation.
Catheter ablation is curative in the great majority and is increasingly offered early.

name: Ventricular Arrhythmias
tagline: Rhythms arising below the bundle of His, ranging from benign ectopy to ventricular fibrillation and sudden cardiac death.
overview: Ventricular arrhythmias originate in ventricular myocardium or the distal conduction system. They range from isolated ventricular ectopic beats, which are common and usually benign, through non-sustained and sustained ventricular tachycardia, to ventricular fibrillation — a disorganised rhythm that produces no cardiac output and is the immediate mechanism of most sudden cardiac deaths. The critical clinical distinction is between arrhythmias occurring in a structurally normal heart, which are generally of good prognosis, and those occurring in the presence of scar, cardiomyopathy or an inherited channelopathy, which carry a substantial risk of sudden death.

modifiable: Electrolyte disturbance, especially potassium and magnesium
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
nonModifiable: Inherited channelopathies such as long QT and Brugada syndromes
Genetic cardiomyopathies including ARVC and HCM
Family history of sudden cardiac death

pathophysiology.title: Scar-related re-entry
pathophysiology.text: Surviving myocyte bundles within and around infarct scar conduct slowly and anisotropically, creating fixed circuits that sustain monomorphic ventricular tachycardia.

pathophysiology.title: Triggered activity
pathophysiology.text: Early afterdepolarisations occurring during a prolonged repolarisation phase can trigger torsades de pointes; delayed afterdepolarisations from calcium overload underlie some catecholaminergic arrhythmias.

pathophysiology.title: Abnormal automaticity
pathophysiology.text: Ischaemic or injured Purkinje and ventricular tissue can develop enhanced spontaneous depolarisation and generate ectopic rhythms.

pathophysiology.title: Channelopathy substrate
pathophysiology.text: Inherited abnormalities of sodium, potassium or calcium handling alter action potential duration and dispersion of repolarisation, creating vulnerability without structural disease.

pathophysiology.title: Degeneration to fibrillation
pathophysiology.text: Wavebreak and multiple wandering wavelets replace organised activation. The ventricles quiver, cardiac output ceases, and death follows within minutes without defibrillation.

pathophysiology.title: Haemodynamic collapse
pathophysiology.text: Even organised ventricular tachycardia at rapid rates severely limits filling; with poor ventricular function it rapidly causes hypotension and loss of consciousness.

anatomyInvolved: Ventricular myocardium, particularly peri-infarct border zones
Purkinje network, a source of triggering ectopy
Right ventricular outflow tract, the commonest site of idiopathic ventricular tachycardia
physiologyChanges: Loss of coordinated ventricular activation, producing a wide QRS complex
Severely shortened diastolic filling with markedly reduced stroke volume
Loss of atrioventricular synchrony, causing cannon a waves and variable first heart sound
Complete loss of cardiac output in ventricular fibrillation
Prolonged or abnormal repolarisation in channelopathies

progression.text: Isolated premature ventricular complexes; frequently benign, but a very high burden can cause cardiomyopathy.
Three or more consecutive ventricular beats lasting under 30 seconds. Prognostic significance depends entirely on the underlying substrate.
Lasting 30 seconds or longer, or requiring intervention. Usually indicates significant structural disease.
Chaotic activity with no output. Immediate defibrillation is the only effective treatment.

symptoms: Palpitations or an awareness of skipped beats
Presyncope and syncope, often without warning
Sudden collapse with no preceding symptoms in ventricular fibrillation
signs: Rapid regular pulse in monomorphic VT; absent pulse in VF
Cannon a waves and variable first heart sound from atrioventricular dissociation
Hypotension, poor perfusion and reduced consciousness
Cardiac arrest with absent pulse and respiration

investigations.findings: Wide-complex tachycardia; features favouring VT include AV dissociation, capture and fusion beats, and extreme axis. Assume a wide-complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise.
Quantifies ectopic burden and documents non-sustained episodes.
Identify structural substrate — scar, cardiomyopathy, ARVC — with late gadolinium enhancement being particularly informative.
Coronary imaging or functional testing, since ischaemia is a common and treatable trigger.
Where a channelopathy or inherited cardiomyopathy is suspected, with cascade screening of relatives.
Substrate mapping and inducibility testing; enables ablation of the critical isthmus.

complications: Sudden cardiac death
Hypoxic brain injury after resuscitated arrest
Recurrent shocks and electrical storm in ICD recipients
Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy from high ectopic burden
Psychological consequences including anxiety and post-traumatic stress

treatment.principles: Acute management follows resuscitation algorithms: immediate defibrillation for pulseless VT and VF, and synchronised cardioversion for unstable VT with a pulse. Long-term management centres on treating the substrate, correcting reversible triggers, and defibrillator implantation for those at high risk. Educational summary only — follow current resuscitation guidelines and local protocols.

groups.name: Immediate resuscitation
groups.detail: High-quality CPR and prompt defibrillation, following current advanced life support algorithms.

groups.name: Reversible cause correction
groups.detail: Revascularisation for ischaemia, correction of potassium and magnesium, withdrawal of QT-prolonging drugs.

groups.name: Antiarrhythmic drugs
groups.detail: Beta-blockers are foundational; amiodarone and other agents are used for suppression, with awareness of proarrhythmia.

groups.name: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator
groups.detail: For secondary prevention after a survived arrest and for primary prevention in defined high-risk groups.

groups.name: Catheter ablation
groups.detail: For recurrent monomorphic VT, electrical storm and idiopathic outflow tract or fascicular tachycardias.

groups.name: Family screening
groups.detail: Clinical and genetic evaluation of relatives when an inherited condition is identified.

keyTakeaways: Treat any wide-complex tachycardia as ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise.
AV dissociation, capture beats and fusion beats strongly favour VT over SVT with aberrancy.
Prognosis depends far more on the underlying substrate than on the arrhythmia itself.
Ventricular fibrillation is the immediate mechanism of most sudden cardiac deaths; only defibrillation reverses it.
Always search for reversible triggers: ischaemia, electrolytes and QT-prolonging drugs.
A sustained ventricular arrhythmia should prompt evaluation of the patient's family.

name: Conduction Disorders & Bradyarrhythmias
tagline: Failure of impulse generation or transmission — from sinus node dysfunction to complete atrioventricular block.
overview: Conduction disorders result from failure at any point in the pathway from sinus node to Purkinje network. Sinus node dysfunction produces inappropriate bradycardia, pauses or chronotropic incompetence. Atrioventricular block is graded first, second or third degree, and the level of block — within the AV node or below it — determines both prognosis and the need for pacing. Nodal block is often vagally mediated, responds to atropine and may be benign; infranodal block is unpredictable, tends to progress, and generally requires pacing. Bundle branch and fascicular blocks are usually markers of underlying disease rather than problems in themselves.

modifiable: Rate-slowing drugs — beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, amiodarone
nonModifiable: Increasing age with idiopathic fibrosis of the conduction system
Prior cardiac surgery or transcatheter valve intervention
Infiltrative disease such as amyloidosis and sarcoidosis

pathophysiology.title: Age-related degeneration
pathophysiology.text: Progressive fibrosis and calcification of the conduction system — historically termed Lev's and Lenègre's disease — is the commonest cause of acquired block in older adults.

pathophysiology.title: Ischaemic injury
pathophysiology.text: Inferior infarction may cause nodal block through AV nodal artery involvement or increased vagal tone; this is usually transient. Anterior infarction causing block implies extensive septal necrosis and carries a worse prognosis.

pathophysiology.title: Nodal versus infranodal block
pathophysiology.text: Block within the AV node produces a narrow-complex escape at 40–60 per minute and often improves with atropine. Infranodal block yields a slow, unreliable wide-complex escape at 20–40 per minute.

pathophysiology.title: Wenckebach physiology
pathophysiology.text: In Mobitz type I block, progressive fatigue of nodal conduction lengthens the PR interval until a beat fails, after which the node recovers and the cycle repeats.

pathophysiology.title: Escape rhythm dependence
pathophysiology.text: In complete block, atrial and ventricular activity become dissociated and the ventricles depend entirely on a subsidiary pacemaker, which may be slow, unreliable or absent.

pathophysiology.title: Haemodynamic consequences
pathophysiology.text: Bradycardia reduces cardiac output when stroke volume cannot compensate; loss of atrioventricular synchrony reduces filling and produces cannon a waves. Long pauses cause syncope, and prolonged asystole causes death.

anatomyInvolved: Sinuatrial node and the surrounding atrial tissue
Atrioventricular node in the triangle of Koch
Bundle of His and its branches within the interventricular septum
Fascicles of the left bundle and the Purkinje network
Coronary supply to the nodes — sinuatrial and AV nodal arteries
physiologyChanges: Reduced heart rate with a fall in cardiac output when stroke volume cannot compensate
Loss of atrioventricular synchrony and of the atrial contribution to filling
Prolonged PR interval, dropped beats, or complete atrioventricular dissociation
Dependence on subsidiary pacemakers with slower and less reliable intrinsic rates
Widened QRS when the escape focus lies below the bundle of His

progression.text: PR interval greater than 200 ms with every impulse conducted. Usually asymptomatic; marked prolongation can impair AV timing.
Progressive PR prolongation until a beat is dropped. Usually nodal and often benign.
Sudden non-conducted P waves without PR prolongation. Usually infranodal, unpredictable, and an indication for pacing.
No atrioventricular conduction; atria and ventricles beat independently. Requires pacing unless a clearly reversible cause is found.

symptoms: Dizziness, presyncope and syncope, often abrupt and without warning (Stokes–Adams attacks)
Reduced exercise capacity from chronotropic incompetence
Often entirely asymptomatic and found incidentally
signs: Cannon a waves in the jugular venous pulse in complete block
Variable intensity of the first heart sound
Wide or paradoxical splitting of the second heart sound in bundle branch block
Hypotension and signs of poor perfusion if severe

investigations.findings: The primary test — PR interval, pattern of dropped beats, QRS width and escape rhythm rate all localise the level of block.
Holter, patch and implantable loop recorders to capture intermittent block, particularly in unexplained syncope.
Potassium, thyroid function, digoxin level, and inflammatory or infective markers including Lyme serology in the right setting.
Identifies structural heart disease and infiltrative cardiomyopathy.
Assesses chronotropic competence and whether block worsens with exercise, which suggests an infranodal level.
His-bundle recording precisely localises the site of block when non-invasive testing is inconclusive.

complications: Syncope with injury
Asystole and sudden death
Bradycardia-induced heart failure
Ventricular arrhythmia in the setting of profound bradycardia and QT prolongation
Pacemaker-related complications including lead problems, infection and pacing-induced cardiomyopathy

treatment.principles: Identify and reverse the treatable — drugs, electrolytes, ischaemia, infection — then decide whether permanent pacing is required based on symptoms and the level of block. Educational summary only; follow current guidelines and resuscitation protocols.

groups.name: Reversible cause management
groups.detail: Withdraw offending drugs, correct hyperkalaemia and hypothyroidism, treat ischaemia and infection.

groups.name: Acute measures
groups.detail: Atropine for nodal block, chronotropic infusions, and temporary transcutaneous or transvenous pacing for haemodynamically significant bradycardia.

groups.name: Permanent pacing
groups.detail: For symptomatic sinus node dysfunction, Mobitz II and complete block; single- or dual-chamber devices selected by rhythm and clinical need.

groups.name: Physiological pacing
groups.detail: His-bundle and left bundle branch area pacing preserve native activation and reduce the risk of pacing-induced cardiomyopathy.

groups.name: Cardiac resynchronisation
groups.detail: Considered where a high burden of ventricular pacing is expected in patients with impaired ventricular function.

keyTakeaways: The site of block matters more than the degree: nodal block is often benign, infranodal is not.
Mobitz I shows progressive PR prolongation; Mobitz II shows sudden dropped beats.
A narrow escape at 40–60 per minute suggests a junctional origin; a wide escape at 20–40 suggests ventricular.
Always exclude drugs, hyperkalaemia, ischaemia and hypothyroidism before implanting a pacemaker.
Block after inferior infarction is usually transient; after anterior infarction it implies extensive damage.
